title: 25  Model Selection and Comparison
text:
Exercises

25.1. Using the Drug A/B Cox partial likelihood from Exercise 23.1, perform a likelihood ratio test of \(H_0: \beta = 0\) against \(H_1: \beta \neq 0\).


Click here to see hints.

Simplify \(\ell(\hat\beta) - \ell(0)\) by cancelling the \(\log(1/24)\) terms. Use \(\log(4/3) = \log 4 - \log 3\) and collect terms.

The partial log-likelihoods are: \[\ell(0) = \log\!\left(\tfrac{1}{24}\right) - 4\log 2, \qquad \ell(\hat\beta) = \log\!\left(\tfrac{1}{24}\right) - \log 3 - 4\log\!\left(\tfrac{4}{3}\right).\]

Compute the likelihood ratio test statistic \(T = -2(\ell(0) - \ell(\hat\beta))\).
State the null distribution of \(T\) and the critical value at the 5% level.
State your conclusion. Is it consistent with the Wald test in Exercise 23.2?

25.2. When analysing survival data, one must often choose between a fully parametric model (e.g., Weibull PH) and the semi-parametric Cox model.

Which of the following is an advantage of the Cox model over a Weibull PH model?
Advantage of the Cox model: No assumption about the shape of the baseline hazard is neededThe Cox model always gives more precise parameter estimatesThe Cox model can be fitted without any censored observationsThe Cox model gives explicit estimates of the survival function at arbitrary future times without additional estimation
Which of the following is an advantage of the Weibull PH model over the Cox model?
Advantage of the Weibull model: The Weibull model makes no distributional assumptionsWhen the model is correctly specified, parametric estimates are more efficient and allow direct survival prediction at any future timeThe Weibull model is always preferred when the sample size is largeThe Weibull model cannot be used when there are tied event times
Suppose you fit both a Weibull PH model and an exponential PH model to the same data. Since the exponential model is the Weibull with shape \(\gamma = 1\), the two models are nested. The deviances (\(-2 \times\) log-likelihood) are: Weibull \(= 83.4\), Exponential \(= 89.2\). Use a likelihood ratio test (i.e. the change in deviance) to decide whether the extra shape parameter is justified.

26.4 Step 3: Fit the Cox model
We fit a series of nested Cox models and select the best using the LRT.


Code
M0 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ 1,                 data = h, ties = "breslow")
M1 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age,               data = h, ties = "breslow")
M2 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ nephrectomy,       data = h, ties = "breslow")
M3 <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ age + nephrectomy, data = h, ties = "breslow")

# LRT: age effect
cat("Age (M1 vs M0):", -2*(M0$loglik[2] - M1$loglik[2]),
    "df=2, p =", pchisq(-2*(M0$loglik[2] - M1$loglik[2]), 2, lower.tail = FALSE))

# LRT: nephrectomy conditional on age
cat("Nephrectomy | age (M3 vs M1):",
    -2*(M1$loglik[2] - M3$loglik[2]),
    "df=1, p =", pchisq(-2*(M1$loglik[2] - M3$loglik[2]), 1, lower.tail = FALSE))

26.5 Step 4: Interpret the final model

Key results from the final model:

Age 60–70 vs \(<60\): \(\hat\psi \approx 1.01\) (95% CI: \([0.44,

Age \(>70\) vs \(<60\): \(\hat\psi \approx 3.83\) (95% CI: \([1.20,

title: 26  Survival Analysis: Extended Case Study
text:
26.6 Step 5: Diagnostics


Code
# Schoenfeld residual test
ph_test <- cox.zph(M3)
print(ph_test)
plot(ph_test)

# Deviance residuals
dev_res <- residuals(M3, type = "deviance")
plot(seq_along(dev_res), dev_res, type = "h",
     xlab = "Patient index", ylab = "Deviance residual")
abline(h = c(-2, 2), lty = 2, col = "red")


The cox.zph() test should show no significant time trends for age or nephrectomy, confirming the PH assumption. Most deviance residuals should lie within \(\pm 2\).

title: 26  Survival Analysis: Extended Case Study
text:
26.7 Step 6: Comparison with parametric model
As a sensitivity analysis, we compare with a Weibull PH model.


Code
# Weibull model (requires survreg with AFT -> PH conversion)
wei_fit <- survreg(Surv(time, status) ~ age + nephrectomy,
                   data = h, dist = "weibull")
summary(wei_fit)
gamma_hat  <- 1 / wei_fit$scale
beta_ph    <- -gamma_hat * coef(wei_fit)[-1]
exp(beta_ph)   # hazard ratios


The Weibull model provides additional shape information (\(\hat\gamma\)) and should yield similar hazard ratio estimates to the Cox model if the Weibull fit is reasonable.

title: 26  Survival Analysis: Extended Case Study
text:
26.8 Summary
This case study has demonstrated the complete survival analysis workflow:

Exploratory analysis: KM curves by group reveal patterns.
PH assumption check: log-cumulative hazard plots support PH.
Model selection: LRT identifies which covariates to include.
Interpretation: hazard ratios quantify covariate effects.
Diagnostics: Schoenfeld residuals and deviance residuals confirm model adequacy.
Sensitivity analysis: comparison with parametric model confirms robustness.

The finding that nephrectomy substantially reduces hazard (by ~76%) is clinically meaningful and consistent with established medical knowledge. The strong age effect (\(>70\) group) highlights that patient age is an important prognostic factor in kidney cancer.
